earth_uses: Increased fuel efficiency in practical combustion devices.
Reduced pollutant emission in practical combustion devices.
Better combustion modeling to help designers improve efficiency and cut harmful pollutants.
profile.experiment_goal: SLICE set out to learn how flow conditions and combustion chemistry cause a flame to detach from the burner and stabilize downstream, in order to advance combustion modeling for greater fuel efficiency and lower pollutant emissions.

glossary.definition: The near-weightless condition on the ISS where gravity's pull is greatly reduced.
A flame that leaves the burner and burns at a spot farther downstream.
Air that flows alongside the fuel jet in the same direction.
Tiny solid carbon particles formed when a fuel burns incompletely.

open_questions: Soot control remains one of the major unsolved problems in combustion and engine development (D1 p14).

profile.summary_expert: SLICE (Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment) studied lifted and lifting flames in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) on the ISS. Flow conditions and combustion chemistry cause the flame to detach from the burner and stabilize at a downstream position. The study used SPICE hardware and ran 12 tests in 2012. Fuels included 100% CH4, 70% CH4 (balance N2), 40% CH4 (balance N2), 20% C2H4 (balance N2), 100% C2H6, and 100% C2H4. The twin purposes were increased fuel efficiency and reduced pollutant emission in practical combustion devices, and to advance combustion modeling capability. SLICE is a second-generation follow-on to the ELF investigation and a precursor to the CLD Flame experiment. Oxygen percentage, pressure, and airflow ranges are not reported in the sources.
profile.summary_simple: SLICE studied flames that lift off a burner and float downstream in microgravity. Scientists ran it on the space station in 2012. They wanted to understand how flow and chemistry make a flame detach and settle at a new spot. Learning this helps build cleaner, more fuel-efficient burners on Earth.
